entries.clue: A bit of wonderment to block short mound (6)

indicatorNotes.to block: Blocking a gap means sitting in the middle of it, so one piece lodges inside the other instead of beside it.
indicatorNotes.short: Short asks for the word beside it cut before it finishes, one letter fewer than it normally runs.

blocks.note: wonderment is awe, the feeling of being struck by something
a mound is a HILL, cut short of its last letter

annotation.surface: Somebody's amazement getting in the way of a small hillock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A bit' measures time here rather than quantity: you wait a bit, you wait awhile. Wonderment is the ordinary crossword awe, a word grids love for its three cheap vowels.
annotation.definitionFit: To stay awhile is to stay a bit — both name a short, unmeasured stretch of time.

entries.clue: Coastal workers' footwear (6-7)

blocks.note: the people who gather winkles, the small edible sea snails, off the rocks at low tide
the needle-toed shoes of the late fifties, sharp enough to pick a winkle out of its shell

annotation.surface: The boots worn by people whose job keeps them on the shore.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe makes the two halves read as one phrase, which is the whole disguise. Winkle-pickers were the pointed shoes of the Teddy boys and the early Beatles.
annotation.definitionFit: Winkle-pickers gather winkles from the rocks; winkle-pickers are also the sharply pointed shoes British teenagers wore in the late 1950s.

entries.clue: Unlawful sick one linked with never-ending place (7)

indicatorNotes.never-ending: Something never-ending has no end, so the word it describes gives up its final letter.

blocks.note: off sick and feeling ill are the same complaint
the Roman numeral for one
a place is a CITY, and with no ending it stops at CIT

annotation.surface: An unwell person tied to somewhere that goes on forever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Linked with' only joins the pieces and hands over no letters of its own. 'Place' for a city is deliberately vague — a setter can call almost any settlement a place, and the crossings decide which one.
annotation.definitionFit: Illicit describes what the law forbids — an illicit still, an illicit deal — so unlawful is a straight swap.

entries.clue: Poles in error get a letter for the Greeks (7)

indicatorNotes.error: An error is something gone wrong, and letters that have gone wrong are letters out of their proper order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: Polish people who have blundered being handed a letter meant for Greece.
annotation.walkthrough: Capitalised 'Poles' invites you to think of Warsaw, or of north and south; it is only letters to be rearranged. The small word 'in' belongs to the fodder rather than to the joining, which is where the seventh letter comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: Epsilon is the fifth letter of the Greek alphabet, so 'a letter for the Greeks' names it by the alphabet it belongs to.

entries.clue: Lower the value of French headquarters (6)

blocks.note: de is French for 'of', as in Simone de Beauvoir
an army runs its operations from its base, the headquarters in the field

annotation.surface: Talking down the worth of a French head office.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of' looks like the hinge of the sentence and is a word to be translated instead. Debasing a coinage once meant literally mixing cheap metal into it.
annotation.definitionFit: To debase a currency is to lower what it is worth, and the word keeps that sense for a reputation too.

entries.clue: Evil spirit lurking inside monastery! (5)

indicatorNotes.lurking: To lurk is to wait out of sight, so the answer is sitting unseen in the words that follow rather than being spelt out.

blocks.note: five letters in an unbroken run, starting four letters into the first word and crossing the gap into the second

annotation.surface: Something wicked hiding in a religious house.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark sells the shock and helps the eye skate over the join between the two words. Hidden answers are the one kind that hands you every letter in order, so the whole difficulty lies in not seeing them.
annotation.definitionFit: A demon is an evil spirit in the plainest sense, the thing an exorcist is called out for.

entries.clue: Fish one caught is the fundamental ingredient (5)

indicatorNotes.caught: Something caught is held fast inside whatever caught it, so the letter named lands within the word beside it.

blocks.note: bass is the fish, the sea bass on every menu
the Roman numeral for one

annotation.surface: An angler landing the fish the whole dish is built on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caught' belongs to the fishing on the surface and does the holding in the parse. The fish and the double bass are spelt the same and said differently, a trap this clue leaves alone.
annotation.definitionFit: The basis of a sauce or an argument is what everything else is built on, the ingredient you could not take out.

entries.clue: Primary outfit? (6,7)

blocks.note: read as chief or most important, and meant as the primary school, where British children go until eleven
read as any set of clothes, and meant as the particular set a school insists on

annotation.surface: The most important set of clothes somebody owns.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing here comes apart into letters: 'primary' has to stop meaning chief and become the school. The question mark is the setter's signal that the phrase is being stretched.
annotation.definitionFit: A school uniform is the outfit a school requires, and in Britain the primary school is where a child first has to wear one, so the whole clue describes it.

entries.clue: American icon man clues badly (5,3)

indicatorNotes.badly: Something done badly comes out wrong, and letters that come out wrong are not in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Somebody making a poor job of setting his crossword clues.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Badly' sits at the end where an anagram indicator likes to sit, and the words in front of it run to exactly the eight letters wanted. Uncle Sam is the white-bearded figure in the star-spangled top hat from the recruiting poster.
annotation.definitionFit: Uncle Sam is the personification of the United States, the figure the country gets drawn as, which is what makes him an American icon.

entries.clue: Some lasso horses in an area of London (4)

indicatorNotes.Some: Some of a thing is a part of it, so only a run of the letters in front is wanted and not the lot.

blocks.note: four letters in a row, running out of the end of the first word and into the start of the second

annotation.surface: A cowboy roping horses in the middle of London.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Some' is the quietest of the hidden-word signals and reads easily as part of the picture. Soho is the square of streets north of Shaftesbury Avenue, long the home of London's clubs, film industry and sex trade.
annotation.definitionFit: Soho is a district of the West End, so 'an area of London' names it by example.

entries.clue: Endlessly obstruct an alliance (4)

indicatorNotes.Endlessly: Endlessly means without an end, so the last letter of the word it governs is dropped.

blocks.note: to obstruct a road is to BLOCK it, and the word loses its final letter

annotation.surface: Getting in the way of something for good.
annotation.walkthrough: The two words differ by a single letter, which makes this the gentlest deletion in the puzzle and the easiest to miss for that reason. A bloc is a group of countries or parties acting together — the Eastern bloc, a voting bloc.
annotation.definitionFit: A bloc is a set of states or members that line up together on an issue, which is an alliance.

entries.clue: Desires something spicy, but without much hope (4,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a noun and the definition a phrase describing how something is attempted; the setter is leaning on the idiom, since a long shot is precisely the try made in that spirit.

blocks.note: to long for something is to desire it
a hot curry is the spicy one

annotation.surface: Someone craving a fiery meal and not expecting to get one.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface hints at odds or risk; 'hope' does the defining while pretending to belong to the meal. A long shot was first a shot fired from too far off to be likely to hit.
annotation.definitionFit: A long shot is an attempt with slim odds of coming off, so it is what you try when you have little hope of it.

entries.clue: Cooking vessel held by boy, exactly (4,2)

indicatorNotes.held by: What is held by something sits inside it, so the vessel goes within the word that follows rather than next to it.

blocks.note: a boy in the family is somebody's son
a pot is what goes on the stove

annotation.surface: A lad carrying the saucepan.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boy' is one of those small words a setter can spend a dozen ways — son, lad, cub, page — and only the crossings say which. Spot on is British for dead right.
annotation.definitionFit: Spot on means precisely right — a spot-on impression, a spot-on guess — which is what 'exactly' says.

entries.clue: Quiet loathing for a platform (6)

blocks.note: p for piano is the musician's mark for quiet
odium is hatred, the contempt a disgraced name attracts

annotation.surface: Silent hatred aimed at a stage.
annotation.walkthrough: The quiet is the musical p printed under the stave, one of the most reliable single letters in the crossword language. Odium is the public sort of loathing, the kind that attaches to a name after a scandal.
annotation.definitionFit: A podium is the small raised platform a speaker or a conductor stands on.

entries.clue: Exercise, sharp turns possibly? (7)

indicatorNotes.turns: To turn is to change into something else — milk turns, fortunes turn — so the letters beside it come out as a different word.

blocks.note: PE, physical education, is the school lesson of running about
five letters shuffled

annotation.surface: A gym session with some sharp changes of direction in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' reads as a hedge on the exercise and is in fact the definition. PE has meant physical education on every British school timetable for a century, and crosswords use nothing else for it.
annotation.definitionFit: Perhaps and possibly are the same hedge — perhaps it will rain, possibly it will rain — interchangeable in any sentence.

entries.clue: Winner of French drink (7)

blocks.note: de is the French word for 'of'
cider, the drink pressed from apples

annotation.surface: The champion among French drinks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of' is the sentence's hinge and the word to be translated, which is the whole of the first two letters. Cider is drunk hard in Normandy as well as the West Country, so the surface holds together.
annotation.definitionFit: In football the goal that settles a match is called the winner or the decider indifferently — he scored the winner, he scored the decider.

entries.clue: Quickly view level - that's insufficient (8)

annotation.definitionNote: Scantier is a comparative and 'insufficient' is not; the clue asks you to hear 'less than enough' in the definition and supply the extra step yourself.

blocks.note: to scan a page is to run the eye over it fast
a tier of a cake or a stadium is one level of it

annotation.surface: A hurried look at one shelf, and it does not come to enough.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Level' is a noun here, not the adjective or the verb, which is where a solver loses time. The dash does the work a link word would do and hands over nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: Something scanty falls short of what is wanted — a scanty meal, scanty evidence — so the answer names what is insufficient.

entries.clue: Heavyweight returning to church to make a mark (5)

indicatorNotes.returning: Something returning comes back the way it went, so those letters are read in the opposite direction.

blocks.note: a ton is a great weight, and it comes back the other way as NOT
ch is the standard short form of church, as printed on a map

annotation.surface: A boxer going back to church to leave his mark.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heavyweight' offers the boxer and means a literal ton. In a down entry a thing that returns is travelling upwards, so the weight is read from the bottom of those squares.
annotation.definitionFit: To notch something is to cut a nick in it, the tally mark scored on a stick, which is making a mark in the plainest way.

entries.clue: Desperate to win, but trailing behind (2,3)

indicatorNotes.Desperate: A desperate person is past all order and method, and letters in that state will not stay as they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters

annotation.surface: A competitor throwing everything at victory and still coming last.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Desperate to win' is such a natural phrase that the two words after it are hard to hear separately, which is where fodder likes to hide. In tow is the state of a broken-down car or a small child at the supermarket.
annotation.definitionFit: Something in tow is being pulled along behind — a caravan in tow, children in tow — which is trailing behind.

entries.clue: Piece of film gets cut (4)

blocks.note: a short extract, the bit of a movie shown on a chat show
the shears verb, used of a hedge, a hairstyle or a coupon taken out of a newspaper

annotation.surface: A section of a movie being taken out in the edit.
annotation.walkthrough: The noun is what has been cut out and the verb is the cutting, which is why the line reads as one sentence about editing. A clip is also the fastener you clip papers with, a third sense left out of play.
annotation.definitionFit: A clip is a short extract from a film, and to clip is to cut — the shears sense the extract is named from.

entries.clue: Put one's feet up with others (4)

blocks.note: stopping work and taking the weight off, the armchair end of the day
the remaining ones, everybody in the group not already counted

annotation.surface: Relaxing in company.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are everyday words and neither is disguised; the work is seeing that 'with' joins two definitions rather than building a charade. The second sense takes 'the' in front of it in real speech, which the clue quietly leaves off.
annotation.definitionFit: To rest is to put your feet up and stop; and the rest of a group is the others in it, the ones not yet accounted for.

entries.clue: Predator distressed showing sign of sadness (8)

indicatorNotes.distressed: A distressed thing is in disarray — distressed furniture is knocked about on purpose — so the letters come out of order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: A hunting animal in trouble and close to tears.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Distressed' reads as the predator's own state, which is the reversal the surface is selling: the hunter upset rather than the hunted. One long word doing nothing else in the sentence is the usual shape of an anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: A teardrop is the single tear on the cheek, the visible sign that somebody is crying.

entries.clue: Avoid ewes straying around church (6)

indicatorNotes.straying: Sheep that stray wander out of their proper places, and so do the letters they are spelt with.
indicatorNotes.around: Around puts a piece on both sides of another, so the shuffled letters close over what follows.

blocks.note: four letters shuffled, ready to be opened up
ch is the map-maker's short form of church

annotation.surface: Sheep wandering loose round a country churchyard.
annotation.walkthrough: The sheep are shuffled first and the church goes into the result, which is the order the two instructions have to run in. Eschew is the formal word for keeping deliberately clear of something — eschew violence.
annotation.definitionFit: To eschew a thing is to keep away from it on purpose, which is what avoiding it means.

entries.clue: Cut back on wave from south (6)

blocks.note: s is south on any compass or map
to crimp hair is to press a row of tight waves into it

annotation.surface: Trimming a swell rolling in from the south.
annotation.walkthrough: The compass point is the giveaway, once you stop reading the line as weather. Crimping is what hot tongs do to hair, and it is the only wave in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: To scrimp on something is to use less of it than you should — scrimp on ingredients, cut back on ingredients.
